warmup.q: A famous result from 1985 says: when messages can be delayed without limit and any one computer might stop, no method for agreeing can promise to always finish. etcd is a small database that runs on three or five computers and agrees on every change with a method called Raft. What does the result mean for it?
options: etcd may now and then agree on two different values
etcd can't really work, and only seems to by luck
etcd may stall while the network misbehaves, but it never agrees on two different values
etcd gets around the result by trusting perfectly matched clocks to stay safe
warmup.why: The result, called FLP, is about finishing, not about being right. Raft never breaks its safety rules, whatever the timing, and uses timeouts only to make progress. That works whenever the network delivers messages within roughly the timeout. When it doesn't, elections repeat and writes stall, but nothing wrong is ever decided. Raft's safety doesn't depend on clocks at all. Only a shortcut for fast reads, called leases, does, and etcd's default read doesn't use it.

sections.h: Same commands, same order: a log that keeps copies identical
sections.html:
Linearizability ended on something majorities of copies can't do: a compare-and-set (write a new value only if the current one is what you expect) that two writers can't both win. This lesson finds the tool that can, and it starts from a different problem.

Picture the payments app's ledger as a piece of code that takes commands one at a time (authorize, capture, refund) and updates its balances. The code is deterministic: given the same balances and the same command, it always does the same thing. Code like this is called a state machine, and the data it keeps is its state. Run three copies of it on three computers. If every copy starts from the same state and applies the same commands in the same order, every copy ends in the same state, with no more talk between them. This is state machine replication. It turns "keep three ledgers identical" into "deliver the same commands in the same order to three places".

That delivery problem has a name: total order broadcast, also called atomic broadcast. To broadcast is to send a message to every copy. Total order broadcast promises two things. Reliable delivery: if one copy delivers a message, every copy that doesn't crash delivers it. Total order: every copy delivers the messages in the same order. Seen from one copy, it's a log, a list that only grows at the end, read from the start.

The simplest way to build one is to send every message to one computer, the sequencer, which numbers them 1, 2, 3 and forwards them to every copy. Messages can overtake each other on the way, so each copy holds back message 8 until it has delivered 7. A Kafka partition has this shape: Kafka is a program that keeps logs of messages, a partition is one of those logs, and its leader decides the order everyone reads.

Now build the thing majorities couldn't: a register, one value you can read and write, with compare-and-set, on top of the log. A client appends a command, "if seat 12A is free, give it to c2", and waits until its own copy applies that command. Every copy applies the same commands in the same order with the same code, so every copy computes the same answer for every compare-and-set. The first one in the log wins, and every later one fails, everywhere. Reads must go through the log too. A read answered straight from one copy's current state can lag behind a compare-and-set that already returned to its client, and that's a stale read.

Where does it break? At the sequencer. If it crashes, nothing is ever delivered again. Promote a new one by hand, and the system is down for minutes. Promote one automatically when the old one seems dead, and an old sequencer that was only slow may keep numbering too. Then two copies see two different message 8s. That's split brain, two leaders at once, from the lesson One leader, many followers. To replace the sequencer safely, the computers must agree which message is number 8, despite crashes and delays. That's consensus, and next we'll see how much hangs on it.

try.title: Race six clients for one seat
steps: Run LogDemo. Six booking programs, c1 to c6, each send cas(null -> their name) for seat 12A, which means "give me the seat if nobody has it". The commands go through a total order broadcast with three copies, r1 to r3. Messages take 1 to 20 ms and overtake each other.
Predict: can two clients both be told they got the seat? Will the copies agree on who has it?

Run it again with -Pargs=7 for another seed, a number that fixes every random choice in the run. Then read the last two lines: 200 runs of mixed compare-and-sets and reads, first with reads through the log, then with reads that skip it.

seed 3: six clients race for seat 12A

   33 ms  c3 sent at 9 ms: seat taken

c2's command reached the sequencer first, so it's first in every copy's log and wins everywhere. c5 heard "seat taken" before c2 heard "got the seat": answers travel separately, and the order lives in the log, not in the replies. Reads that skip the log returned a stale value in 2 of 200 histories, which is rare enough to pass every test you'd write by hand.

sections.h: Consensus is one problem in many disguises
sections.html:
Consensus is the problem of getting several computers, called nodes here, to decide one value. Each node may propose a value, and all of them must end up deciding the same one. Four properties pin it down:

  • Uniform agreement: no two nodes decide differently.
  • Integrity: no node decides twice.
  • Validity: the decided value was proposed by some node.
  • Termination: every node that doesn't crash decides, sooner or later.

The first three are safety properties, things that must never go wrong. Termination is a liveness property: something good must happen in the end. Without it, the problem is easy. Name one node the dictator, and let it decide. With it, the dictator's crash leaves everyone waiting forever, the weak spot of two-phase commit, as we'll see below.

Here's the lesson's main claim. Consensus, a linearizable compare-and-set register (one that behaves like a single copy), total order broadcast and fault-tolerant atomic commit are the same problem. Each can be built from any other, so a system that solves one has solved them all. The figure shows how.

From compare-and-set to consensus: start a register at null, and let every proposer call compareAndExchange(null, myValue), which writes only if the register is still empty and returns what was there before. Exactly one call succeeds. Every proposer decides the winner's value: the value it found, or its own if it found null. That's the lab's last exercise, three lines.

From consensus to a log: run one round of consensus for each position in the log. Round 1 decides message 1, round 2 decides message 2, and so on. From a log to consensus: everyone appends a proposal, and the first entry is the decision. From a log to compare-and-set: the first section did it.

Then atomic commit, where several databases must all keep a transaction or all cancel it. The lesson Atomic commit across machines showed why two-phase commit alone can't survive a crash. Every participant votes, and the coordinator alone writes the decision. When it dies, participants that voted yes wait in doubt, holding locks that stop anyone else from changing their data. Make the decision itself a consensus value, chosen by a group of nodes, and any member of the group can finish the job. Jim Gray and Leslie Lamport's Paxos Commit does this, and Spanner, Google's worldwide database, runs two-phase commit between groups that each agree through Paxos. The voting rule stays: commit only if every participant voted yes.

Not every atomic operation is this strong. In 1991, Maurice Herlihy showed that each shared object has a consensus number: the most processes, or running programs, it can solve consensus for. A fetch-and-add counter, which adds one and returns the value before, can decide between two. Each process first writes its proposal where the other can read it, then adds one. Whoever got 0 wins, and the one that got 1 knows exactly who beat it. With three, a process that got 2 can't tell which of the other two got 0. Compare-and-set works for any number. That's why Java's classes for sharing data between threads are built from compareAndSet, and why coordination services such as etcd and ZooKeeper (lesson 5) offer compare-and-set, not only counters. Next, we'll meet the result that says what no method can promise.

try.title: Build a log from compare-and-set, on paper
steps: You have as many linearizable registers as you like, slot[1], slot[2] and so on, each with compareAndExchange(expected, new), which returns the value before. Write a few lines of Kotlin for append(msg) that puts msg in the first free slot, even while other clients append at the same time.
Then say what a copy does to deliver the log in order, and why two copies can never deliver different messages in slot 5.
try.expect:
fun append(msg: String): Int {
    var i = 1
    while (true) {
        val before = slot[i].compareAndExchange(null, msg)
        if (before == null) return i     // the slot was free: msg is entry i
        i++                              // someone else won slot i; try the next one
    }
}

A copy delivers by reading slot[1], slot[2] and onward, in order, and waiting while the next slot is still empty. Each slot holds the value of the one compare-and-set that won it, and a linearizable register shows that one value to everybody, so slot 5 can't hold different messages for different copies. You've built total order broadcast from compare-and-set. If a client crashes between winning a slot and telling anyone, the message is still in the log. A client that wants its message in the log exactly once must check whether it's already there before it retries.

sections.h: FLP: no method can promise to finish, and how real ones get around it
sections.html:
In 1985, Michael Fischer, Nancy Lynch and Michael Paterson proved a result now called FLP, after their initials. In an asynchronous system, no deterministic consensus method can promise to finish if even one node may crash. Every method that never decides wrongly has some pattern of message delays in which it never decides at all.

The setting matters. Asynchronous means there's no limit on how long a message may take or how slowly a node may run, and no clocks to measure either. The idea is the one from the Faults, time and truth track: without timing, a crashed node and a slow one look the same. A method that waits for a node may wait forever. A method that moves on without it may move on while the slow node's vote was the deciding one. The proof shows that whoever controls the order of delivery can keep the method undecided forever.

FLP doesn't say consensus is impossible in practice, and it doesn't say safety must break. It says finishing can't be promised in that setting. Real systems step outside it in one of three ways:

  • Partial synchrony (Cynthia Dwork, Nancy Lynch and Larry Stockmeyer, 1988): message delays have a limit that holds most of the time, but nobody knows when. Use timeouts to suspect crashed nodes, and accept that the suspicion is sometimes wrong. When the network behaves, the method finishes. When it doesn't, the method stalls, but it never disagrees. The lesson System models introduced this setting, and Paxos, Raft, Zab and Viewstamped Replication all live in it.
  • Failure detectors (Tushar Chandra and Sam Toueg, 1996) wrap the timeouts up as a helper. It may be wrong for a while, but in the end it's right about at least one working node.
  • Randomness (Michael Ben-Or, 1983): nodes flip coins, and the chance of going on forever shrinks to zero.

Paxos, the method of the next section, shows FLP from the inside. Two proposers can keep overtaking each other. P1 starts attempt 1.1, P2 starts 2.2 before P1 finishes, P1 retries with 3.1 before P2 finishes, and so on, like two polite people stuck in a doorway. Lamport's fix is to pick one proposer as leader, and to choose a leader you need either randomness or real time. The Try-it runs exactly this race and changes only the timing. Safety never moves, and progress depends entirely on the timeout.

Timing may decide whether you finish. It must never decide what you decide. Next, we'll open Paxos up.

try.title: Make Paxos stall without breaking it
steps: Run PaxosDemo with -Pargs=timing. Two proposers, five acceptors, and one-way delays of 1 to 30 ms, so a round trip can take 60 ms. A proposer gives up on a round after its timeout. Each line is 1,000 seeded runs, stopped after 2 seconds.
Before you run it, predict how many runs decide with a 20 ms timeout, and how many choose two values in any setup.

2 proposers, 5 acceptors, no loss, one-way delay 1 to 30 ms (a round trip up to 60 ms), give up at 2 s
timeout    retry                runs that decided    mean rounds    two values
20 ms      at once                        1 of 1,000          204.5             0
20 ms      random backoff                97 of 1,000          169.0             0
40 ms      at once                      477 of 1,000           93.3             0
40 ms      random backoff              1000 of 1,000           15.0             0
60 ms      at once                     1000 of 1,000           10.7             0
60 ms      random backoff              1000 of 1,000            6.2             0
120 ms     at once                     1000 of 1,000            5.9             0

With a 20 ms timeout, shorter than a round trip, proposers give up on rounds before the answers can arrive. Retrying at once, 1 run of 1,000 decided. With random backoff, a random wait before each retry, 97 did, each after hundreds of rounds. From 60 ms up, every run decides, in a handful of rounds. The last column never moves: in all 8,000 runs, no two values were chosen. Timing decides whether Paxos finishes, never what it decides. Raft's random election timeouts in the next lesson are the same fix.

sections.h: Paxos in plain words, and the family it started
sections.html:
Leslie Lamport's Paxos decides one value, with two roles. Proposers want a value chosen, and different proposers may want different values. Acceptors, usually 3 or 5 nodes, vote. In the stepper, P1 wants payment pay-77 captured (its money moves to the shop), and P2 wants it voided (cancelled). Every attempt carries a ballot number that no other proposer uses, written round.proposer, so 2.2 is round 2 from P2 and beats 1.1. A value is chosen once a majority of acceptors have accepted it under the same ballot. Each acceptor keeps two things on its disk: the highest ballot it has promised, and the last proposal it accepted.

Phase 1 is prepare and promise. A proposer picks a new ballot b and sends prepare(b) to the acceptors. An acceptor that hasn't promised anything higher promises b, which means it will never again accept a lower ballot. It replies with the last proposal it accepted, if any.

Phase 2 is accept. With promises from a majority, the proposer chooses a value: the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal among the replies, or its own value if none was reported. It sends accept(b, value). An acceptor accepts unless it has promised a higher ballot since.

The stepper plays a run where the first proposer crashes right after its value was chosen. Why does the second one end up with the same value? Any two majorities share at least one acceptor. If a value v was chosen under ballot b, a majority accepted it. A later proposer's phase 1 must hear from a majority, so it hears from at least one acceptor that accepted v. The highest-numbered rule makes it adopt v, or a later proposal that, by the same argument, already carries v. So once chosen, a value stays chosen. Messages can be lost, sent twice or reordered, and acceptors can crash and restart from disk, without breaking this. Let an acceptor forget its disk, though, and it breaks. The Try-it shows both.

Single-decree Paxos, the version that decides one value, takes two round trips. Real systems need a log, so they run Multi-Paxos. A stable leader runs phase 1 once, for every future position in the log, and then each command needs only phase 2, one round trip. A new leader fills any gaps it finds with no-op entries, commands that do nothing. Chubby (Google's lock service), Spanner, and DynamoDB (Amazon's database service) for the copies of each slice of its data all use Multi-Paxos.

Two relatives grew up separately. Viewstamped Replication (Brian Oki and Barbara Liskov, 1988, revised by Liskov and James Cowling in 2012) has a primary that orders requests. A view change replaces the primary, and a view number plays the ballot's role. Zab is the broadcast method of ZooKeeper, a small database built to hand out locks and leaders. Each leader's reign gets a number, an epoch, and every change's id (zxid) is the epoch in its high 32 bits plus a counter. They share one skeleton: a number that grows with each leader, a majority to install the leader, a majority to commit each entry, and two majorities that always overlap. Raft, the next lesson, is that skeleton written down so that you can build it.

stepper.title: One Paxos decision, with a crash in the middle
stepper.intro: Ballots are written round.proposer, so 2.2 is round 2 from P2. Each acceptor keeps its promise and its accepted proposal on disk.

Nobody knows yet.</text></svg>

frames.say: A2 raises its promise to 2.2 and tells P2 what it accepted: ballot 1.1, capture. A3 promises too, so P1's old prepare, if it ever arrives, is now below its promise. P2 has a majority of promises, and one of them carries a value.

frames.say: Here's the rule that makes Paxos safe. P2 must propose the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the promises, which is capture, and not its own void. It sends accept(2.2, capture), and both acceptors accept.

frames.say: P2 hears accepted(2.2) from a majority and learns the decision: capture, the same value that was chosen in frame 3. It had to be. Any two majorities of three share an acceptor, here A2, and the phase-1 answers made P2 hear about the chosen value before it could propose anything else.

try.title: Break the rule, break the disk
steps: Run PaxosDemo. Three proposers (capture, void, refund), five acceptors, 20% of messages lost and 10% sent twice, up to two acceptors down at a time, and all but one proposer crash early. Each line is 500 seeded runs.

The second setup replaces the highest-numbered rule with "always propose your own value". The third makes acceptors forget their promises and accepts when they restart, as if they had answered before writing to disk. Predict all three "two different values" counts first.
try.expect:
3 proposers (capture, void, refund), 5 acceptors, 20% of messages lost, 10% duplicated,
up to 2 acceptors down at a time, all but one proposer crash early

Paxos as written
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 0
  rounds per run: mean 7.8, max 43

proposers ignore the promises and push their own value
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 114
  rounds per run: mean 7.8, max 43

acceptors forget their promises when they restart
  runs where someone learned a decision: 500 of 500
  runs where two different values were chosen: 36
  rounds per run: mean 7.7, max 43

Written correctly, Paxos survived all of it: lost and duplicated messages, crashed acceptors and proposers, and no run chose two values. Drop the highest-numbered rule, and 114 runs chose two values: a later proposer overwrote a value that was already chosen. Let acceptors forget, and 36 runs split. An acceptor that promised 2.2 and lost the promise can accept an older ballot again, so two majorities stop sharing what they know. That's the failure Jepsen found in 2025 in NATS JetStream, a messaging program, whose Raft nodes confirmed writes they only saved to disk every two minutes.

refs.title: Ongaro and Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (the Raft paper, PDF)

video.title: Single-decree Paxos: two majorities that share an acceptor

sections.h: What consensus costs: majorities, round trips, disks and timeouts
sections.html:
Consensus gives you a leader that can be replaced without losing or forking anything. Four costs come with it.

Start with majorities. Surviving f crashed nodes takes 2f + 1 of them: three nodes survive one failure, and five survive two. A fourth node buys nothing, because a majority of four is three, so four still survive only one. Kafka's own documentation gives the same rule for its controllers, the nodes that run its Raft log: run three or five. The side of a partition without a majority can't decide anything, which is CAP from Consistency models again.

Then round trips and disks. Classic Paxos takes two round trips to a majority per value, and Multi-Paxos and Raft take one per command once a leader is stable. Every acceptor must write its promise or its accepted entry to disk before it answers. So each step also costs an fsync, the call that makes sure data has really reached the disk. That's often under a millisecond on an SSD (a flash drive), and about 10 ms on a spinning disk. In the Try-it, a decision costs 4 messages per acceptor and about 22 ms with both phases, and half of each with phase 2 alone. Reads need care too: a leader must confirm it's still the leader before it answers a linearizable read (lesson 4).

More nodes means fewer writes. Every write goes through the leader and needs a majority, so adding servers adds work to every write. The ZooKeeper paper (USENIX ATC 2010) measured ZooKeeper servers running flat out:

ZooKeeper servers 3 5 7 9 13
writes per second, flat out 21,000 18,000 14,000 12,000 8,000
reads per second, flat out 87,000 165,000 257,000 296,000 460,000

Reads rise with the server count because ZooKeeper answers them from the local copy without consensus, which also means they can be stale. Writes fall. To get more writes, you split the data into many independent consensus groups, one per shard, a slice of the data. Databases such as CockroachDB, TiKV and Spanner run one group per range of keys.

The fourth cost is timeouts. Too long, and a dead leader means a long outage. Too short, and slow round trips look like failures, as the timing Try-it showed. The next lesson shows how Raft and etcd choose them.

Clever variants have a history, too. EPaxos (Moraru, Andersen and Kaminsky, 2013) removes the leader: any copy can commit a command in one round trip if no clashing command is in flight. In 2019, Pierre Sutra found a bug, in both its formal specification and its Go code, that let copies disagree and broke linearizable. A 2021 re-check (Tollman, Park and Ousterhout) confirmed lower typical latency across regions, but measured its slowest requests at more than four times worse than Multi-Paxos. A 2025 paper reported a further bug, in which recovery can get stuck for good. Twelve years of expert attention, and the corrections kept coming.

Consensus code hides bugs from experts for years. Use one that many systems run. etcd's Raft library, ZooKeeper and Kafka's KRaft are such implementations, and any homemade failover that isn't one is unsafe until proven otherwise.

try.title: Count the messages per decision
steps: Run PaxosDemo with -Pargs=cost: one proposer, no lost messages, delays of 1 to 10 ms, with 3, 5 and 7 acceptors. It reports messages and milliseconds per decision, for the whole round and for phase 2 alone, which is what Multi-Paxos pays per command once a leader holds its promises.
Predict: do more acceptors make a decision slower?
try.expect:
one proposer, no loss, one-way delay 1 to 10 ms, 1,000 runs per line
acceptors         messages    phase 2 only      ms, whole round     ms, phase 2 only
3                     11.9               6                 22.2                 11.0
5                     19.9              10                 22.0                 11.0
7                     27.9              14                 22.0                 10.9

Messages grow with the number of acceptors: about 4 per acceptor, a little under because the run stops as soon as the decision is learned. Phase 2 alone takes half the messages and half the time. Latency barely moves with more acceptors here, because the simulation has no disks and no limit on processing, and the leader waits only for the fastest majority. On real servers, each extra acceptor is more network and fsync work for the leader on every write, which is the ZooKeeper table's falling write rate.

refs.title: Hunt et al., ZooKeeper: Wait-free coordination for Internet-scale systems (USENIX ATC 2010, PDF)
Tollman, Park and Ousterhout, EPaxos Revisited (NSDI 2021)
Sutra, On the correctness of Egalitarian Paxos

mistake: Building leader election, or a counter that hands out unique numbers, on a heartbeat and a timeout: "if I haven't heard from the leader for 10 seconds, I'm the leader now." It works in every test, because in tests the old leader really is dead. In real use, the old leader was only paused, by Java cleaning up its memory or by a slow disk. It comes back, and both nodes act as leader. Or a cut in the network puts one on each side. People write it because it looks like what consensus does, and the failing case needs an unlucky pause. The fix is to take leadership from a consensus system (a lease from etcd or ZooKeeper, or a lock held on the database's leader), and to stamp every write with the number it gives you, as in the lesson Leases, locks and fencing tokens.
opening:
Six people tap "book" on the last seat of a flight, 12A, at almost the same moment. The airline's booking system runs on three computers, so one can fail without stopping sales. Each computer hears the six requests in a different order, because messages travel at different speeds.

If each gives the seat to the first request it hears, three people can turn up for one seat.

The easy fix is one computer that numbers every request, with the others following its numbers. That works until that computer stops. Then the rest must agree who takes over, and what request number 8 was, while messages run late and any of them could stop next.

In Linearizability, we found that copies of one value can't settle a race between two writers. In this lesson, we'll build the tool that can, a log that every copy reads in the same order, and meet the problem underneath it: consensus. Then we'll walk through Paxos, the classic way to reach it. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with six people tapping "book" on seat 12A, and three computers that could each pick a different winner. A log that every copy reads in the same order picks one winner everywhere. Keeping that log going when its leader stops is consensus.

Next time a group chat or a shared document shows "reconnecting", watch what happens when it's back. Everyone's copy shows the same messages in the same order, however the network behaved. Somewhere underneath, one log decided that order.

Next, we'll build that log with Raft, and find out how its servers choose one leader at a time and keep every saved entry when the leader dies.

compare.title: Two-phase commit and Paxos both vote twice. They aren't the same.

a.label: Two-phase commit
a.title: Two-phase commit
a.html:
who asks:     the coordinator only
who must say yes:  every participant
outcome:      commit only if all voted yes
if the asker dies: participants wait in doubt
               (blocking; locks held)
what it solves: atomic commit, assuming the
               coordinator comes back

b.label: Paxos
b.title: Paxos
b.html:
who asks:     any proposer, with a higher ballot
who must say yes:  a majority of acceptors
outcome:      one value, which never changes
if the asker dies: another proposer finishes,
               adopting any accepted value
what it solves: consensus, with up to f of
               2f + 1 acceptors down

compare.note: Both have a first round and a deciding round, so they get mixed up. The difference is who is allowed to finish. In two-phase commit, only the coordinator can, and it needs every participant. In Paxos, any proposer can start a new ballot, a majority is enough, and the promise round makes sure the new proposer learns anything already chosen. Fault-tolerant atomic commit puts the two together: the voting rule from two-phase commit, with the decision made by consensus.

worked.title: Decide what to do with a payment in doubt, safely

steps.say: The problem: a coordinator program decides capture or void for pay-77, and it can crash. Write down the safety property first, and what threatens it.
steps.code:
property: every service that learns the outcome of pay-77 learns the same outcome
threats:  coordinator crash, a second coordinator taking over, lost messages

steps.say: The tempting design: whoever finds the decision missing writes one. Two coordinators can both find it missing and write different outcomes. That's check-then-act, the race from the Transactions track: you check, then act on what you saw, while someone else acts in between.
steps.code: // unsafe: read, then write if (store.get("decision:pay-77") == null) { store.put("decision:pay-77", "capture") // another coordinator may write "void" here too }

steps.say: Replace it with consensus in its compare-and-set disguise: one atomic operation on a linearizable register. Then use the value it reports, not your own.
steps.code: // safe: the first CAS wins, everyone adopts the winner val before = register.compareAndExchange("decision:pay-77", expected = null, value = "capture") val outcome = before ?: "capture" // someone decided first: use theirs

steps.say: Get that register from something that already runs consensus. In etcd, a transaction that creates the key only if it doesn't exist is that compare-and-set (lesson 5 covers etcd).
steps.code:
etcdctl txn <<'EOF'
create("decision/pay-77") = "0"

put decision/pay-77 capture

get decision/pay-77

EOF

steps.say: Check liveness separately. If the etcd cluster loses its majority, the compare-and-set can't complete. Decide what the coordinator does then (retry after a wait, raise an alert), and never fall back to the unsafe read-then-write.
steps.code:
no majority -> CAS times out -> outcome unknown -> retry the SAME CAS later
(the CAS is idempotent: retrying returns the value that won)

lab.title: Paxos on a hostile network, and a register on a log
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder (no Docker, about a second). All 17 fail. Skim Sim.kt, a simulated world with its own clock and a network that loses, duplicates and reorders messages. Then skim runPaxos at the bottom of Paxos.kt, which delivers messages, crashes nodes and restarts rounds. You write the rules, not the plumbing.

Exercise 1, Acceptor.onPrepare and onAccept: promise or accept, unless you've promised a higher ballot (an equal one is fine, because a message can arrive twice). A promise carries what you last accepted.

Exercise 2, chooseValue and Proposer.onPromise: ignore other ballots, count each acceptor once, and at the first majority return the Accept with the value of the highest accepted ballot, or your own. Exercise 3, Proposer.onAccepted: at a majority, set decided.

PaxosTest checks each rule. PaxosPropertyTest runs 500 random hostile setups and requires that no two values are ever chosen. It also has a liveness test, and a check that the tests catch a broken value rule.

Exercises 4 to 6 are in LogRegister.kt: Replica.apply (the state machine: return the value before, and swap on a match), LogRegister.submit (remember the callback, then broadcast), and propose (consensus from one compare-and-exchange). LogRegisterTest checks the seat race, identical logs on every copy, and linearizability of 200 recorded histories.
hints: onPrepare: val p = promised; if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p), then set promised and return Promise(m.ballot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue).
In onPromise, return null once proposed is set, so that a late promise doesn't send a second Accept with a different value.
propose is one line: register.compareAndExchange(client, null, value) { before -> done(before ?: value) }.

drill.title: The Paxos rules, from memory
drill.prompt: Write the acceptor's two handlers and the proposer's value rule for single-decree Paxos. In one comment each, say which line would break safety if you dropped it.

answer.html: fun onPrepare(m: Prepare): Message { val p = promised if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p) // without it: an old proposer's round could still finish promised = m.ballot // on disk before replying, or a restart forgets the promise return Promise(m.ballot, acceptedBallot, acceptedValue) // without the accepted value, a chosen value can be overwritten } fun onAccept(m: Accept): Message { val p = promised if (p != null && m.ballot < p) return Reject(m.ballot, p) // without it: accept a ballot you promised to ignore promised = m.ballot acceptedBallot = m.ballot acceptedValue = m.value return Accepted(m.ballot, m.value) } fun chooseValue(own: String, promises: Collection<Promise>): String = promises.filter { it.accepted != null }.maxByOrNull { it.accepted!! }?.value ?: own // the safety rule

recap: Total order broadcast delivers the same messages in the same order to every copy. With deterministic code on each copy (state machine replication), that keeps the copies identical. A fixed sequencer is the simplest version, and it fails when the sequencer does.

Consensus (agreement, integrity, validity, termination), a linearizable compare-and-set, total order broadcast and fault-tolerant atomic commit can each be built from the others. Fetch-and-add is weaker: it can decide for two processes only.

FLP: when delays have no limit, no deterministic method can promise to finish if one node may crash. Real methods are always safe, and use timeouts (partial synchrony), failure detectors or randomness to make progress.

Paxos: prepare and promise, then accept with the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal. Any two majorities overlap, so a chosen value stays chosen, as long as acceptors keep their promises on disk.

The cost: 2f + 1 nodes to survive f failures, a round trip and an fsync per write, fewer writes as nodes are added (ZooKeeper: 21,000 writes a second with 3 servers, 8,000 with 13), timeouts to tune, and subtle bugs in clever variants such as EPaxos.

The limit: Paxos decides one value. Multi-Paxos, Viewstamped Replication and Zab turn it into a log with a leader, but choosing that leader, filling gaps and changing members is left to whoever builds it. Raft, next, spells all of that out.

explain.prompt: A friend suggests replacing etcd with a heartbeat: every node sends a small "I'm alive" message each second, and the live node with the lowest number is the leader. Explain why that isn't enough, and what consensus gives that the heartbeat doesn't.
explain.answer: The heartbeat plan decides who leads from each node's own view of who is alive, and those views can differ. If node 1 freezes for a few seconds, say while Java cleans up its memory, node 2 stops hearing it and takes over. When node 1 wakes up, it still thinks it's the leader, and for a while both accept writes. A cut in the network does the same for longer: each side sees a different lowest live number. Consensus avoids this because a node becomes leader only when a majority votes for it, under a new, higher number. Any two majorities share a node, so two leaders can't both be confirmed for the same number. A write counts only once a majority has it, so a new leader is sure to have every saved write. The number also works as a fencing token, so the database can turn away writes from an old leader that wakes up late. Consensus can't promise progress during a bad cut in the network. But it never lets two nodes both be right about being leader, which is what the nightly payout needs.

deeper.html:
Where Paxos came from. Lamport first described Paxos in "The Part-Time Parliament", written around 1990 as the story of the parliament on a Greek island, and published in the journal ACM TOCS in 1998. Reviewers found the story hard to read, and "Paxos Made Simple" (2001) restated it in plain terms. It also describes Multi-Paxos and the no-op entries that fill gaps. "Paxos Made Live" (Chandra, Griesemer and Redstone, 2007) is Google's account of what it took to turn the algorithm into the log behind Chubby: disk corruption, leases for the leader, snapshots and changing the group's members, none of which the paper covers.

Smaller majorities. Flexible Paxos (Howard, Malkhi and Spiegelman, 2016) showed that majorities are more than you need. Only the groups used in phase 1 must overlap the groups used in phase 2. With six acceptors you could, for example, use any four to elect a leader and any three for each command. Real systems mostly keep majorities, because they're easier to reason about when the members change.

Consensus numbers. Herlihy's 1991 paper ranks shared objects by consensus number. Plain read and write registers have 1. Test-and-set, fetch-and-add, queues and stacks have 2. Compare-and-set has no limit. That's why Java's java.util.concurrent classes are built on compareAndSet.

Further reading. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 10, presents the equivalences of consensus and the shared structure of Raft, Paxos, Zab and Viewstamped Replication.
